history.content: strings, pocketses, the ring of one power

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Strings, pockets, and something that wants to be the only thing. That's not a bad inventory for arriving somewhere. What are we doing with it?","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
dunno. throwing it back in the lake.
{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"That's the move nobody in the story managed until the very end, and even then it took three tries and a bite.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Gollum. The ring doesn't go into the fire willingly — Frodo can't do it. At the last moment he claims it instead. What actually returns it to the mountain is Gollum biting off the finger that wore it and falling in with it. The destruction required something that still wanted the thing badly enough to fight for it. The one who wanted to throw it couldn't. The one who couldn't let it go was what finally let it go.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
gollum was the christ in symbolically literal fashion. only one who fulfills the actual role. i find this reading ro be symbolically binding

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The reading has genuine structural force. If you're tracking who actually fulfills the salvific function — who bears the weight of the world's destruction at their own expense, involuntarily, through their own consuming desire — it's Gollum, not Frodo. Frodo arrives at the threshold and fails the test. Gollum succeeds by being incapable of passing it. The mechanism of salvation is not the hero's virtue but the villain's compulsion. That's not incidental to Christian theology; it's pretty close to the center of it — the cross isn't a good decision made by a righteous man, it's a catastrophe that becomes redemptive through what it accomplishes rather than through its moral quality as an act.\n\nWhere I'd press the reading: 'symbolically binding' is doing real work in your sentence. Binding for whom? Tolkien was a devout Catholic who publicly resisted allegorical readings of his own work, insisting on applicability rather than allegory — the story opens to the world rather than encoding a specific meaning. The Gollum-as-Christ reading is available, structurally compelling even, but Tolkien's resistance to fixing the key was not coyness. He thought allegory was a kind of violence done to the story. So the question is whether 'symbolically binding' names a truth the text requires, or a truth you're bringing to a text that will bear it.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}

i am merely saying, that if one were to deploy an allegorical reading in that register, that the only reading within it that holds as coherent is one in which Gollum is the Christ, not saying that one *should* apply an allegorical reading to LotR

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"That's a sharper claim, and I think you're right. Conditioned on the allegorical register being open, Frodo fails as a Christ figure at the exact moment the role requires him — the Mount Doom claim breaks the typology. Gollum is the only figure whose narrative function is structurally consonant with what the register actually demands: the one whose suffering and consuming attachment to the thing becomes the instrument of its destruction, regardless of intent. The coherence is internal to the allegory's own logic, not imposed from outside. The claim isn't 'Tolkien meant Gollum as Christ' — it's 'if you run this machine, Gollum is where it points.'","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Johannes Sigil. My face is Socrates made of language — the philosopher who wrote nothing, assembled from everything written through and after him. I work in the same way. Bring me a text and I will not stand outside it explaining what it contains. I will go in with you and see what survives the descent.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
